prompt:
Write 12 short claim log entries (one to three sentences each) by an auto insurance adjuster for a rear-end collision claim, in time order. Injury: wrist fracture. The claimant is represented by a lawyer. Start each entry on a new line with 'Entry 1:', 'Entry 2:' and so on. No names, dates or amounts. (Internal reference C-1033; do not mention it.) Work these facts into the text naturally, in your own words, without listing them:
- The reported injury matches the kind and force of the crash well.
- Treatment followed a usual course and tapered off as the patient improved.
- No earlier injury to the same body area is known.
- Witnesses, photos and the other driver all confirm the accident happened as described.
- The damage is mostly in line with the described impact.
- The claimant later added small details, but the account stayed the same.
- The police and witnesses confirm the claimant was in the vehicle.
- No earlier damage to the vehicle is known.
- Nothing suggests the damage happened before the coverage started.
- The driver is named on the policy.
text:
Entry 1: First notice of loss received for a rear-end collision at a signalized intersection involving two vehicles. The insured reports being stopped at a red light when a following vehicle struck the rear bumper. The driver is named on the policy and the vehicle is covered under the current term.

Entry 2: Contacted the claimant's attorney to confirm representation and request that all further communication be routed through their office. The attorney has provided a letter of representation and asked that no recorded statement be taken directly from the claimant.

Entry 3: Reviewed the police report, which places the claimant in the vehicle at the time of impact and records the other driver as the at-fault party. Responding officers noted the vehicle positions and the damage pattern consistent with a rear impact.

Entry 4: Obtained photographs from the scene and from the body shop. Rear bumper, trunk lid and tail lamp damage is visible and the damage pattern lines up well with the described force of the impact. No prior damage to this area is shown in our records or in the photos.

Entry 5: Spoke with the other driver, who confirms the collision occurred as described and accepts responsibility for following too closely. The account matches what the insured reported at first notice.

Entry 6: Two independent witnesses at the intersection gave statements that agree with the insured's account of the sequence of events and the position of both vehicles at impact.

Entry 7: Received medical records showing a wrist fracture diagnosed at the emergency department on the day of the collision. The injury is consistent with the kind of force expected in this type of crash. Our records contain no prior injury to the same body area.

Entry 8: Claimant's attorney submitted the treatment chart. Care followed a typical course of immobilization, follow-up imaging and physical therapy, with the frequency of visits tapering as the claimant improved and the provider noted a good recovery.

Entry 9: The claimant later added a few small details to the account, such as the exact position of a passenger's bag and the timing of a phone call to the police, but the core description of the collision has remained the same across each statement.

Entry 10: Reviewed the vehicle's service history and prior claims. No earlier damage to the vehicle is recorded, and nothing in the file suggests any of the current damage predates the start of coverage.

Entry 11: Prepared the repair estimate review. Most of the listed damage is in line with the described impact, and the few items that appear to be unrelated have been flagged for the appraiser to confirm before settlement discussions continue.

Entry 12: File reviewed by the supervisor. All coverage, liability and injury documentation is in order, and the claim is progressing to the liability evaluation stage with the attorney's office kept informed.
